title: Body systems that matter in dentistry
blurb: The heart and circulation, breathing, the nervous system and digestion: how they work and where they meet dental care.
question: While a crown is being tried in, it slips from the dentist's fingers to the back of the patient's mouth and the patient coughs, then swallows hard. Moments later, a different patient in the waiting room goes pale and faints after seeing a needle. Which body systems are involved in each case, and what do you need to understand about them?

teach.h: Why a dental nurse needs the whole body
teach.body: The mouth is joined to everything else. A patient's medical history, the drugs they take, how they react to an injection and what happens in an emergency all depend on the body's systems. Four matter most chairside: the cardiovascular system (heart and blood), the respiratory system (breathing), the nervous system (nerves and brain) and the digestive system, which starts in the mouth. Understanding how each works lets you spot when something is going wrong.

steps.label: Right atrium
steps.sub: Deoxygenated blood arrives from the body via the venae cavae

steps.label: Right ventricle
steps.sub: Pumps it to the lungs through the pulmonary artery

steps.label: Lungs
steps.sub: Blood picks up oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide

steps.label: Left atrium
steps.sub: Oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins

steps.label: Left ventricle
steps.sub: Thickest wall: pumps blood out through the aorta

teach.loop: Round the body and back to the right atrium
teach.caption: Valves between the chambers (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) stop blood flowing backwards.

teach.body: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, which is why you can feel a pulse. Veins return blood at low pressure and have valves. Capillaries are tiny vessels where oxygen and nutrients pass into the tissues. Blood is plasma carrying red cells (haemoglobin carries oxygen), white cells (fight infection) and platelets (start clotting). Patients on anticoagulants such as warfarin or apixaban, or antiplatelets such as aspirin, bleed more after extractions, so the dentist needs to know.

items.label: ideal BP (mmHg) is 90/60 to 120/80; 140/90 or above is high

teach.caption: The radial pulse is felt at the wrist and the carotid pulse in the neck. In a collapse, check for normal breathing and never delay CPR to search for a pulse.

teach.body: Air passes through the nose or mouth, the pharynx (throat) and the larynx (voice box) into the trachea (windpipe). The trachea splits into the right and left main bronchi, which branch into smaller bronchioles ending in millions of air sacs, the alveoli, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves. Breathing in is driven mainly by the diaphragm contracting. When we swallow, a flap called the epiglottis covers the larynx so food goes down the oesophagus, not into the lungs.

teach.h: The route of air, and where a dropped object goes

steps.label: Trachea
steps.sub: Rings of cartilage keep it open

steps.label: Right main bronchus
steps.sub: Wider, shorter, more vertical: inhaled objects usually end up here

teach.caption: Protect the airway with high-volume suction, rubber dam and careful handling. If an object may have been inhaled or swallowed, the patient is referred to hospital to be X-rayed.

teach.body: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system is the 12 pairs of cranial nerves (including the trigeminal and facial) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Sensory nerves carry messages in; motor nerves carry instructions out. Local anaesthetic works by stopping a nerve from carrying messages. The autonomic nervous system runs things we don't control consciously, through two opposing halves: sympathetic and parasympathetic.

teach.caption: In a vasovagal faint, a surge through the vagus nerve slows the heart and widens blood vessels, so blood pressure drops and less blood reaches the brain. Lay the patient flat and raise their legs.

teach.h: The digestive system starts in your workplace
teach.body: Digestion begins in the mouth: teeth chew, saliva moistens and amylase starts breaking down starch, and the tongue shapes a bolus to swallow. Food passes down the oesophagus to the stomach, where strong acid and enzymes work on protein, then to the small intestine, where bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas finish digestion and nutrients are absorbed. The large intestine absorbs water. Acid from reflux or repeated vomiting erodes the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth. The liver also breaks down many drugs, including lidocaine.

teach.text: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart, not always oxygenated blood: the pulmonary ARTERY carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. And inhaled objects go to the RIGHT lung more often, because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

items: Heart: right side pumps to the lungs, left side (thickest wall) pumps to the body via the aorta.
Normal adult: pulse 60–100, breathing 12–20 a minute, ideal BP between 90/60 and 120/80 mmHg.
Airway: larynx → trachea → bronchi → alveoli; the epiglottis protects it; inhaled objects favour the right bronchus.
Nervous: CNS plus cranial and spinal nerves; sympathetic = fight or flight, parasympathetic = rest and digest.
Digestion starts in the mouth; acid reflux and vomiting erode the palatal surfaces of upper teeth.

summary: You can now trace blood through the heart, give normal adult observations, follow the route of air to the alveoli and explain why inhaled objects tend to enter the right lung, describe the parts of the nervous system and what sympathetic and parasympathetic activity do (including in a faint), and outline digestion from the mouth onwards, with the dental link for each system.

A.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the body?
A.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and round the body.

whyNot.0: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body.
whyNot.1: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
whyNot.2: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.

A.q: A patient may have inhaled a small instrument. Which part of the lungs is it most likely to have entered?
A.why: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects most often go there.

whyNot.0: The left main bronchus is narrower and angled more sharply, so objects enter it less often.
whyNot.2: The oesophagus leads to the stomach; an object there has been swallowed, not inhaled.
whyNot.3: Objects from the mouth don't travel up into the nasal cavity when inhaled.

A.q: A patient goes pale, sweaty and feels faint after seeing the needle. Which explanation fits?
options: Vagus nerve activity slows the heart
The sympathetic system raises blood pressure
The local anaesthetic has caused an allergy
A.why: In a vasovagal faint, a surge of vagal (parasympathetic) activity slows the heart and widens vessels, so blood pressure falls.

whyNot.1: A sympathetic surge raises blood pressure; a faint is caused by a fall.
whyNot.2: They fainted on seeing the needle, so no anaesthetic has been given yet.
whyNot.3: Fainting is linked to low blood pressure, not raised blood sugar.

B.q: What is a normal resting pulse rate for an adult?
B.why: A normal adult resting pulse is 60–100 beats per minute.

whyNot.2: Above 100 at rest is a fast pulse (tachycardia).
whyNot.3: This is far too fast for a resting adult.

B.q: Which structure covers the larynx during swallowing to stop food entering the airway?
B.why: The epiglottis folds over the entrance to the larynx when we swallow.

whyNot.0: The soft palate rises to close off the nose, not the larynx.
whyNot.1: The uvula hangs from the soft palate and doesn't seal the airway.
whyNot.3: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle below the lungs.

B.q: A patient has frequent acid reflux. Where would the dentist expect erosion?
options: Occlusal surfaces of wisdom teeth only
B.why: Acid from the stomach washes over the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth first.

whyNot.1: Lower incisors are usually the least affected by reflux, shielded by the tongue and saliva.
whyNot.2: Roots are covered by gum and bone unless there is recession.
whyNot.3: Reflux erosion is not limited to wisdom teeth.

C.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
C.why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

whyNot.0: The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body.
whyNot.1: The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
whyNot.2: The venae cavae bring deoxygenated blood from the body to the heart, not to the lungs.

C.q: An anxious patient says their mouth feels very dry before treatment. Which part of the nervous system explains this?
C.why: Anxiety triggers the sympathetic 'fight or flight' response, which reduces saliva and makes it thick.

whyNot.2: Somatic motor nerves move skeletal muscles, not salivary glands.
whyNot.3: Salivary glands are controlled by the autonomic (peripheral) nervous system.

C.q: Where is most digested food absorbed into the blood?
C.why: The small intestine finishes digestion and absorbs most nutrients.

whyNot.0: The stomach breaks food down with acid and enzymes but absorbs little.
whyNot.1: The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach.
whyNot.3: The large intestine mainly absorbs water.

reteach.title: One patient, four systems
reteach.question: Follow one patient through a single appointment and spot each body system at work.

blocks.body: Mrs Khan is nervous: her heart races and her mouth is dry (sympathetic nervous system). You check her medical history and see she takes apixaban, so she may bleed more (blood and clotting). During treatment you keep the suction near the back of the mouth so water and debris don't reach her airway (respiratory). When she rinses and swallows, her epiglottis closes the airway and the water goes down her oesophagus (digestive). Afterwards she stands too quickly and feels dizzy as her blood pressure briefly drops (cardiovascular).

blocks.h: Each system and its dental link
head: System
Dental link
rows: Inhaled objects, asthma, airway in emergencies
Local anaesthesia, anxiety, epilepsy, vasovagal faint

blocks.text: Fight or flight = DRY mouth and a FAST heart. Rest and digest = WET mouth and a SLOW heart.

explain.body: The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps it to the body through the aorta. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries exchange oxygen with the tissues. Platelets start clotting.

test.q: Which part of the blood starts the clotting process after an extraction?
test.why: Platelets clump together at the injured vessel to start forming a clot.

whyNot.1: Clotting factors in plasma help, but platelets start the process by forming a plug.

explain.body: Air travels through the pharynx, larynx and trachea to the bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli, where gas exchange happens. The diaphragm drives breathing. The epiglottis guards the airway during swallowing.

test.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
test.why: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between air and blood across the thin walls of the alveoli.

whyNot.0: The trachea is an airway that carries air to the bronchi.
whyNot.2: The larynx is the voice box at the top of the airway.
whyNot.3: The bronchi carry air into each lung but are too thick-walled for gas exchange.

explain.body: Central: brain and spinal cord. Peripheral: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Autonomic: sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest). Local anaesthetic blocks nerve messages.

children.label: Peripheral
children.sub: 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs; includes the autonomic

test.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there?
test.why: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, including the trigeminal (V) and facial (VII).

whyNot.0: The trigeminal is cranial nerve number 5; there are more pairs than that.
whyNot.1: The facial nerve is number 7, not the total.
whyNot.3: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

explain.body: Mouth (chewing, saliva, amylase) → oesophagus → stomach (acid, protein digestion) → small intestine (bile and pancreatic enzymes, absorption) → large intestine (water). The liver makes bile and breaks down many drugs.

test.q: Where does chemical digestion of starch begin?
test.why: Salivary amylase begins breaking down starch while food is still in the mouth.

whyNot.1: The stomach mainly starts protein digestion.
whyNot.3: The oesophagus moves food by peristalsis but doesn't start digestion.
